items.title: OSINTdefender Army Chief of Staff General Randy George warned in late December, two months before the Iran war began, that the Army was critically short on missile defense munition…
items.summary_raw: OSINTdefender Army Chief of Staff General Randy George warned in late December, two months before the Iran war began, that the Army was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last until 2030, according to multiple U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. The Pentagon says claims of munitions shortages are “false.”  The warning was a risk analysis in the Pentagon’s Global Force Management Allocation Plan for fiscal 2027, which sets where troops and weapons go worldwide, the officials said. They said THAAD and Patriot interceptors would stay strategically low, citing Patriot transfers to Ukraine, munitions used to defend Israel during the 12 Day War and reduced industrial capacity. CBS withheld the exact percentages for security reasons. Gen. George declined to comment.  Officials told CBS the U.S. still holds a significant stock of offensive munitions, such as JDAMs and Small Diameter Bombs, but missile defense interceptors are low. One said even with no further use, restoring the already low December 2025 levels would take until 2030. ATHENS - Josh Huck officially assumed duties as Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, of the U.S. Diplomatic Mission to Greece, on Thursday October 15, 2026. A career member of the U.S. Foreign Service with the rank of Minister Counselor, Chargé d’Affaires Huck previously served as Deputy Chief of Mission at the U.S. Embassy in Athens. In his new capacity, he will lead the Mission’s continued efforts to advance U.S. priorities and further strengthen the longstanding strategic partnership between the United States and Greece. The United States remains firmly committed to its close partnership with Greece, including expanding defense and security cooperation, strengthening regional energy security, promoting trade and investment, and advancing shared interests in the Eastern Mediterranean and beyond.

items.title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
items.summary_raw:
Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia

Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.

Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.

items.title: Golden Dome Is Technologically and Financially Infeasible

items.summary_raw:
US military weighs using 'mother of all bombs' if Trump resumes war

The US military has developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations, CNN reported on Thursday citing US officials familiar with the matter.

The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the conflict, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.

Report by Reuters

items.title: For the future of green politics, look beyond the Green party | Zoe Williams
items.summary_raw:
Environmentalists of all political hues must find the language and ideas that turn passion for climate action into impetus

The future of Green politics is under constant discussion after the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, but a much heavier clash – in meaning, symbolism and portent – happened earlier this summer, in King’s Lynn and West Norfolk. The council declared a climate emergency in 2021, along with hundreds of others, and while it was under Conservative control. It is now controlled by independents, and a Reform UK councillor, Austen Moore, moved to scrap the declaration.

It was the end of June, and the meeting had to be called off, because of the extreme heat in the King’s Lynn council chamber. A lot of people paused to grimly remark on that irony, but not Moore, who simply rescheduled the motion for the following week, where it was voted down (by 33 to seven). items.title: Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year
items.summary_raw:
Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climate

Western Europe’s highest mountain shrank by more than a metre last year. The peak of Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.

The mountain is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.

items.title: I work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisis | Anonymous
items.summary_raw:
Insurers are taking on more risk than they should. If – or when – a major disaster hits, the catastrophe will have far-reaching consequences

I work for a major insurer, assessing the risk posed by natural disasters on properties around the world, from family homes to schools, government offices and multibillion-dollar commercial centres. The world is facing greater risk than ever from extreme weather. We are not prepared – and that inaction could have profound consequences for the global financial system.

In the face of ever more extreme and unpredictable climate risks, I am coming under pressure to cut my forecasts for the losses that disasters will cause in order to make insurance more affordable – and get my employer more business. In some instances, the questioning of our numbers and models is justified. But too often, it is not being done to produce more accurate models, but to artificially lower prices. If this is happening at my firm, which is struggling to compete with rivals’ prices, it’s happening elsewhere.

The writer is a modeller working in the insurance industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journali

items.summary_raw: Two more commercial ships have been targeted by drone strikes just outside Bulgarian territorial waters in the western Black Sea. One of the ships is currently sinking, while the other was damaged.  Shipping data shows that the Turkish-owned "AZOV CONCORD" cargo vessel sunk approximately 17 nautical miles east of Krapets, Bulgaria, while the "CHELSEA 3" cargo ship, which is owned by Ukrainian company "STAR SKY SHIPPING" was damaged approximately 18 nautical miles off the coast of Byala, Bulgaria. "CHELSEA 3" was reportedly hit by three different drones.   The Bulgarian Prime Minister has summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, and is requesting urgent NATO surveillance over the area.

items.title: Trump says Iran wants deal with US but 'don’t know how to'
items.summary_raw:
Trump says Iran wants deal with US but 'don’t know how to'

US President Donald Trump says Iran wants to reach a deal with Washington, but claims "they don’t know how to".

"They want to make a deal, but they don’t know how to,"  he said during a campaign rally in Ohio. 

Trump added that Washington could not allow Tehran to acquire a nuclear weapon, describing the country as "the number one state sponsor of terror".

"Right now, they have no navy, they have no air force, they have no anti-aircraft, they have the worst inflation of any country anywhere in the world, they have no money," the US president said.

items.title: Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?
items.summary_raw:
Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?

Officially known as Ansar Allah, or "helpers of God", the movement emerged in Yemen's far north in the 1990s around the cleric Hussein al-Houthi.

It is rooted in Zaydism, a branch of Shia Islam whose followers are a minority in Yemen but concentrated in the northern highlands.

The group fought six rounds of war with the government of former president Ali Abdullah Saleh between 2004 and 2010. Hussein al-Houthi was killed in the first and leadership passed to his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, who still heads the movement.

items.title: A super el Niño threatens our food system. Here’s how farms can prepare | Liz Carlisle
items.summary_raw:
Planting cover crops or perennial plants can protect soil amid potential flooding. Congress must act to protect these practices

As forecasters warn that this year’s El Niño could become the strongest on record, concerns are growing about its effect on agriculture and food security.

The United States will not be hit nearly as hard as Central and South America, the Caribbean and southern Africa, but severe weather could cause significant crop loss in some parts of the country.

Liz Carlisle is associate professor of environmental studies at UC Santa Barbara. She is the author of Healing Grounds: Climate, Justice, and the Deep Roots of Regenerative Farming and co-editor of Living Roots: The Promise of Perennial Foods

items.title: Archbishop Georgios of Cyprus to Meet with Pope Leo at the Vatican
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA – Archbishop Georgios of Cyprus will visit the Vatican from October 19 to 20, where he will meet with Pope Leo on October 19. Speaking to the state broadcaster RIK, Archbishop Georgios confirmed reports that during the meeting he will request the transfer to Cyprus of the Holy Skull of the Apostle Paul. He also stated that during the meeting he will seek the Pope's assistance regarding the violation of religious freedoms in the occupied part of Cyprus. The Primate of the Church pointed out that he will also seek the support of the Holy See on the Cyprus issue, since it has many accredited ambassadors throughout the world.

items.title: Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
items.summary_raw:
Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea

  • Europe live – latest updates

Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range.

An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling.

items.title: Morning update
items.summary_raw:
Morning update

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

Here are the latest developments: 

  • During a phone call between Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi and his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan, Araghchi insisted that a military approach in Yemen will complicate the situation in the region. According to Iranian state media, Araghchi had also indicated Iran's readiness in helping start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen. 

  • Air strikes were reported on the Hamdan district in Sanaa and two more strikes on al-Zurbi Road in the Hayfan district in Taiz, according to Yemen’s Houthi-run Saba news agency. Missile attacks were also later reported on the border district of al-Dhaher in Saada province.

  • A drone attack on a vessel off the coast of Oman left two Indian nations missing

items.title: Iran security chief accuses Trump of ‘smuggling’ oil through Hormuz
items.summary_raw:
Iran security chief accuses Trump of ‘smuggling’ oil through Hormuz

Iran’s security chief claimed on Sunday that US President Donald Trump's adminitation hired “thugs” in the coastal waters of Oman to smuggle oil through the Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump “claims every day that the Strait of Hormuz is open, but in response I say: ‘You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iranian control and we manage it,'” Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei was quoted as saying by Iran's ISNA news agency.

Rezaei said that the smuggling operation involves the UAE military and the commander of US Central Command (Centcom), using a handful of “small vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers” and that Iran targets them “every night”.
